content.text: An AI-text detector doesn't know who wrote a text. It scores how predictable the text looks to a language model, and plain, careful human writing looks predictable too. In a 2023 study, seven detectors flagged non-native writers' essays as AI-generated most of the time, while one editing prompt let AI text slip through. Treat a score as a weak hint, never as proof.

Your team runs a developer blogging platform, and product asks for an "AI-written" badge to fight spam. You wire up a popular detector API. In the first week it flags a post by Mona, a backend engineer in Cairo who wrote every word herself, in careful, plain English, her second language. The same week, a post a chatbot generated and then reworded on request passes as human. Neither result is a bug in your integration.
The common misconception
"An AI-text detector can reliably tell whether a person or an LLM wrote a text." It sounds reasonable:

items.text: Detectors return a precise-looking score, such as "92% AI", which reads like a measurement.
Unedited chatbot output often does sound generic, and detectors catch much of it.
Published methods report striking numbers, such as a watermark detector that catches 99.8% of AI passages while flagging 1% of human ones.

content.text: It's a half-truth. Unedited output from a known kind of model carries a real statistical signal. It breaks down in the cases that matter: edited text, writers with a plain style, and whether
this
person wrote
this
text.
What actually happens
A detector scores predictability, not authorship
Many detectors start from
perplexity

: run the text through a language model and measure how surprised the model is by each next token. Chat models tend to pick likely tokens, so their raw output has low perplexity. A zero-shot detector sets a threshold on that kind of score; a trained detector learns similar features from examples.

The catch is that low perplexity isn't a fingerprint of AI. Anyone who writes with common words and simple sentence patterns produces it too: people writing in a second language, beginners, technical prose full of standard phrases. The detector can't see who typed the text, only how ordinary the word choices are.
Who gets flagged
Liang and colleagues at Stanford tested seven widely used detectors in March 2023 on 91 TOEFL essays by non-native English writers and 88 essays by US 8th graders. The results:

items.text: The US essays were almost all classified correctly.
The average false positive rate on the TOEFL essays was 61.22%. All seven detectors flagged 18 of the 91 essays, and at least one detector flagged 89 of them.
Asking ChatGPT to enhance the TOEFL essays' word choices cut the false positive rate to 11.77%. Asking it to simplify the US essays raised theirs from 5.19% to 56.65%.

content.text: In ICLR 2023 abstracts, written before ChatGPT was released, authors in non-native English-speaking countries also wrote lower-perplexity text: a property of how people write, not evidence of cheating. The samples were small and most detectors used GPT-2 as their backbone, so today's tools will show different rates; plain wording read as AI is the mechanism to test yours for. The irony the authors note: to avoid being flagged, non-native writers may need AI.
Editing erases the signal

The same study shows the other failure. Detection of 31 essays generated by ChatGPT-3.5 dropped from up to 100% to up to 13% after a single follow-up prompt: "Elevate the provided text by employing literary language".

Sadasivan and colleagues ran about 300-token passages from watermarked OPT models through a paraphrasing model repeatedly. In every setting they tested, two rounds pushed the watermark detector's true positive rate, at a 1% false positive rate, below 50%; five rounds, below 20%. On 50- or 100-token passages, detection after the attack was about as good as random. Human raters still scored the paraphrases 4 or 5 out of 5 more than 70% of the time.
A ceiling no detector can beat

AUROC is the chance a detector ranks a random AI text above a random human one; 0.5 is a coin flip. Sadasivan and colleagues proved that the best possible AUROC shrinks as AI text becomes statistically closer to human text; once the two are close enough, even the best possible detector stays below 0.7. And making a detector stricter about false accusations makes it miss more AI text.
Watermarks only prove what they marked
A
watermark

is a different idea: the model cooperates. In Kirchenbauer and colleagues' scheme, a pseudo-random set of "green" tokens is chosen before each word and the sampler softly favors them; a statistical test later counts green tokens, without access to the model. Google's SynthID Text works as a logits processor in the same spirit, and its detector answers watermarked, not watermarked or uncertain.

Google's documentation lists the limits: the watermark is less effective on factual responses, and confidence can be greatly reduced when the text is thoroughly rewritten or translated. It also covers only models that apply it, so a missing watermark says nothing about a human author.
The arithmetic of a flag

Two calculations show what a flag is worth. The first applies the study's average false positive rates to 50 human-written essays per group; the second asks how many flags land on humans when AI text is the minority.

It prints 3 flagged essays for the US group, 31 for the TOEFL group, then 33%: when most people write their own work, even an accurate-sounding detector accuses an innocent person in one flag out of three.

rows.text: "92% AI" is the chance an AI wrote it
It's a predictability score; plain human writing scores high too
Detectors treat all writers the same
Average 61% false positives on TOEFL essays, about 5% on US 8th graders
Catching raw chatbot output means catching cheaters
One editing prompt cut detection from up to 100% to up to 13%
As models approach human text, even the best detector nears a coin flip
No watermark means a human wrote it
Watermarks cover only cooperating models, and rewriting weakens them

blocks.title: Ask about the process, not the text

content.text: When authorship matters, as in coursework or hiring, ask for drafts, version history or a short conversation about the work. A person who wrote it can explain their choices; a score can't.

Wrong flags aren't spread evenly: in the Stanford study, non-native writers were flagged about twelve times as often as native ones. An automatic penalty turns that gap into discrimination, and most Arab developers who write in English are non-native writers too.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Never automate a decision on a score

content.text: Use a detector, if at all, as one signal that starts a human review. Never as the reason to reject, ban or grade.

items.title: Measure false positives on your own users

content.text: Run the detector on texts you know people wrote, such as posts from before ChatGPT's release in November 2022. Split the results by group: non-native writers, short posts, technical docs. If one group is flagged far more, stop.

If your product generates text, log its outputs or watermark them at generation time. SynthID Text is open source and available in Hugging Face Transformers v4.46.0+. Then "did our system write this?" has a real answer.
Ask people to state how they used AI, and judge the work on its quality and correctness rather than on its origin.
Key takeaways

items.text: A detector measures how predictable a text is, not who wrote it.
Plain, careful writing looks "AI" to detectors: non-native essays averaged a 61% false positive rate in 2023.
A single editing prompt or a paraphrase removes the signal, and the best possible detector weakens as models improve.
Watermarks identify only text from models that apply them; rewriting and translation weaken them.
Never penalize on a score: measure false positives per group and rely on process and disclosure.
